FAQ

How spicy is Thai food really?

It can be very spicy, especially dishes eaten by locals, but it's about balance, not just heat — and you can almost always order milder. In tourist areas dishes are often toned down by default. Plenty of dishes are naturally mild.

How do I order Thai food less spicy?

Say "mai phet" (not spicy) or "phet nit noi" (a little spicy). Note that even "a little spicy" can be hot by Thai standards, so start cautious and build up as you learn your tolerance.

Which Thai dishes are the spiciest?

Som tum (papaya salad), tom yum soup, laab, many curries (especially green and jungle), and Isan/northeastern dishes tend to be hot. Milder choices include pad thai, satay, fried rice, massaman, and tom kha.

What cools your mouth after spicy food?

Plain rice, anything sweet, and dairy or coconut work best — not water, which spreads the chili oil. A sweet Thai iced tea, coconut drink, or cucumber helps tame the heat.

title: Thai Food 101: What to Order as a First-Timer
excerpt: A first-timer's guide to ordering Thai food — the essential dishes to try, how to handle spice, regional specialties, and tips for eating well and safely.
content:
Thai food is one of the great reasons to visit Thailand, and eating your way through the country is a highlight in itself. But the menus can be overwhelming and the spice levels intimidating for first-timers. This guide covers the dishes to order, how to manage the heat, and how to eat well wherever you are.

The essential dishes to try

Start with the classics that define Thai cuisine. Pad Thai (stir-fried rice noodles) is the famous gateway dish. Tom yum goong is the iconic hot-and-sour shrimp soup; tom kha gai is its milder, coconut-based cousin. Green, red, and massaman curries range from fiery to mild and rich. Som tum (green papaya salad) is a punchy, spicy favorite, and pad krapow (stir-fried basil with minced meat over rice, often topped with a fried egg) is the beloved everyday dish Thais eat constantly. Don't leave without trying mango sticky rice, the perfect sweet ending. Beyond these headliners, keep an eye out for khao man gai (Thai-style poached chicken and rice), satay skewers with peanut sauce, and the endless variety of noodle soups sold from stalls — Thai food rewards the adventurous orderer, and pointing at what looks good on a neighbor's table is a perfectly good strategy.

Regional specialties worth seeking out

Thai food changes as you travel. In the north (Chiang Mai), try khao soi, a rich coconut-curry noodle soup, and sai ua, a herby northern sausage. In the northeast (Isan), the famous trio is som tum, laab (a zesty minced-meat salad), and grilled chicken (gai yang) with sticky rice. In the south, expect richer, spicier curries and incredible fresh seafood. Eating regionally is one of the joys of traveling the country.

How to handle the spice

Thai food can be genuinely fiery, but you have control. Learn the phrase "mai phet" (not spicy) or "phet nit noi" (a little spicy) to dial it down. Be aware that "a little spicy" by Thai standards can still be hot for many visitors, so start mild and work up. If a dish catches you out, rice (not water) and something sweet or dairy help most. Over a trip, most people find their tolerance grows — and the chilies are part of what makes the food sing.

Where and how to eat

Some of the best food in Thailand comes from humble places: street-food stalls and simple local restaurants often outshine fancy ones. Look for busy stalls with high turnover (a sign of freshness and popularity), watch your food being cooked fresh, and don't be afraid of the plastic-stool places — they're where Thais eat. A guided street-food tour early in your trip is a great way to learn what's what and discover stalls you'd never find alone.

Vegetarian, vegan, and dietary needs

Thailand is increasingly easy for vegetarians and vegans, though a little care helps. Many dishes can be made meat-free, but fish sauce and shrimp paste are common hidden ingredients, so learn the phrase "jay" (which signals strict vegetarian/vegan, often linked to a Buddhist dietary tradition) or "mang-sa-wirat" (vegetarian). Look for the yellow-and-red "jay" symbol on restaurants, especially during the annual Vegetarian Festival. For allergies, carry a translation card, since cross-contamination at busy stalls is hard to control. With a few key phrases, eating well with dietary restrictions is very doable.

Eating safely

Thai street food is generally safe, and a few habits keep it that way: choose busy stalls where food is cooked fresh and turns over quickly, eat things hot and freshly made, and drink bottled water (ice in established places is usually fine, made from purified water). Give your stomach a day or two to adjust to new spices and ingredients. With a little common sense, eating from stalls is one of the safest and most rewarding things you'll do. Meals are remarkably cheap; check a live converter rather than a fixed figure:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

FAQ

What Thai dishes should a first-timer order?

Pad Thai, tom yum or tom kha soup, a curry (green, red, or mild massaman), som tum (papaya salad), pad krapow (basil stir-fry), and mango sticky rice for dessert.

How do I order Thai food less spicy?

Say "mai phet" (not spicy) or "phet nit noi" (a little spicy). Note that even "a little spicy" can be hot by Thai standards, so start mild. Rice and something sweet help if a dish is too hot.

Is Thai street food safe to eat?

Generally yes — choose busy stalls with high turnover, eat food hot and freshly cooked, and drink bottled water. Street food is often the best and most authentic eating in Thailand.

Does Thai food vary by region?

A lot. The north has khao soi and sai ua, Isan in the northeast has som tum, laab, and grilled chicken, and the south has richer curries and fresh seafood. Eating regionally is a highlight.

title: Getting Around Bangkok: BTS, MRT, Taxis, and Grab
excerpt: How to navigate Bangkok like a local — the BTS Skytrain and MRT metro, river boats, Grab, taxis, and tuk-tuks — and how to beat the city's notorious traffic.
content:
Bangkok's traffic is legendary, and the single biggest factor in enjoying the city is knowing how to move around it. The good news: Bangkok has excellent elevated and underground trains, river boats, and ride-hailing that let you skip the gridlock entirely. Here's how each option works and when to use it.

The BTS Skytrain and MRT metro — your main tools

The BTS Skytrain (elevated) and MRT (underground) are the backbone of getting around modern Bangkok: clean, fast, cheap, air-conditioned, and — crucially — they fly over or under the traffic. Between them they cover most areas a visitor needs: Sukhumvit, Silom, the river, Chatuchak, and major malls. Buy a stored-value card or single-journey tickets at the stations. Staying near a BTS or MRT station is the best transport decision you can make in Bangkok.

River boats — scenic and traffic-free

The Chao Phraya Express Boat and cross-river ferries are the smart way to reach the historic temple area (the Grand Palace, Wat Pho, Wat Arun), which the trains don't directly serve. They're cheap, frequent, and a lovely way to see the city from the water. A tourist boat with a day pass stops at the main riverside sights. Connect from the BTS at Saphan Taksin pier. The orange-flag commuter boats are the cheapest and most frequent, while the blue-flag tourist boat is pricier but stops conveniently at the main riverside sights with English commentary — a good first-day option for getting your bearings on the river.

Grab — the easy door-to-door option

Grab (Southeast Asia's Uber) is the most stress-free way to get door-to-door, especially for places off the train lines or when you're tired or loaded with shopping. You see the price upfront, pay through the app, and avoid any haggling or meter disputes. It's widely used and reliable. Bolt and inDrive are alternatives. For most visitors, Grab plus the trains covers everything.

Taxis and tuk-tuks

Metered taxis are plentiful and cheap if the driver uses the meter — insist on "meter" and avoid any who quote a flat fare. Tuk-tuks (the three-wheeled open-air icons) are fun for a short ride and a photo, but they're not cheaper than a metered taxi or Grab, you have to negotiate hard, and some drivers run gem-shop scam detours. Treat tuk-tuks as an occasional novelty rather than your main transport.

Buses, boats, and motorbike taxis

Bangkok's public buses are very cheap but slow, hot, and hard to navigate without local knowledge — most visitors skip them. Canal boats (on Khlong Saen Saep) are a fast, local way to cut across the city center, if a bit chaotic. Motorbike taxis (riders in colored vests) zip through traffic for short hops and are great for beating a jam, if you're comfortable on the back of a bike for a few minutes.

Getting to and from the airports

Both Bangkok airports are well outside the center. From Suvarnabhumi (BKK), the Airport Rail Link connects to the city and the BTS — the cheapest route if your hotel is near a station — while a metered taxi or Grab is simplest door-to-door, though you'll hit traffic. From Don Mueang (DMK), the budget-airline airport, taxis, Grab, and airport buses are the main options. If you land late and tired, a pre-booked car or a Grab is well worth the few extra dollars to skip the taxi queue and any fare haggling.

How to beat the traffic

The strategy is simple: plan your day around the trains and river boats, use Grab to bridge the gaps, and avoid being in a car on the roads during rush hours (roughly 7–9am and 4–7pm), when Bangkok gridlocks. If you must cross town by road at peak time, allow far more time than the distance suggests. Stay near a Skytrain station and you'll rarely need a car at all. Fares are low across the board; check a live converter rather than a fixed figure:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

FAQ

What's the best way to get around Bangkok?

The BTS Skytrain and MRT metro for most trips (they skip the traffic), river boats for the temple area, and Grab for door-to-door rides. Stay near a station to make it effortless.

Is Grab better than taxis in Bangkok?

For most visitors, yes — Grab shows the price upfront, you pay in the app, and there's no haggling or meter disputes. Metered taxis are fine and cheap if the driver uses the meter.

Should I take tuk-tuks in Bangkok?

For the experience, once — but they're not cheaper than a metered taxi or Grab, require hard negotiation, and some run gem-shop scam detours. Use them as a novelty, not your main transport.

How do I avoid Bangkok's traffic?

Use the Skytrain, metro, and river boats, fill gaps with Grab, and avoid road travel during rush hours (about 7–9am and 4–7pm). Staying near a BTS station means you rarely need a car.

title: Getting Around Thai Islands Without a Scooter
excerpt: What fills the gap if you do not ride — songthaew networks, fares and coverage, island by island.
content:
Not everyone wants to ride a scooter, and on some Thai islands you do not need to. What varies enormously is what fills the gap — a frequent shared-truck network on one island, a handful of charter taxis at fixed rates on another. This is what the alternatives actually look like, island by island.

What a songthaew is

A songthaew is a pickup truck with a covered bed and two bench seats facing each other. On most Thai islands it functions as the closest thing to public transport. Where a genuine network operates, you flag one down, ride along a broadly fixed route, and pay a set fare when you get out.

The word covers two quite different things, though, and the difference matters. On some islands songthaews behave like shared buses: they run set routes, pick up whoever is going that way, and charge per person. On others the same vehicle operates as a chartered taxi — a fixed price for the whole truck, negotiated or posted, whether you are one passenger or four.

Island by island

Koh Samui

Songthaews circle the ring road, which runs about 51 km around the island and passes through most of the main beach towns. Routes follow driver preference more than a published timetable, but the network is real and continuous during daylight. Fares run roughly 30 to 150 baht depending on distance — a wide band, because a hop between adjacent beach towns and a run across the island are both served by the same trucks. Service thins out in the evening, whereas Grab, which also operates here, does not keep those hours.

Phuket

Fixed routes run from Phuket Town out to the individual beaches, roughly 6am to 6pm, at about 15 to 50 baht — the cheapest fares of any island here. The shape of that network matters more than the price, though: it radiates from the town rather than connecting the beaches to each other, so a trip between two neighbouring beaches often means going in and back out, while the same distance on Koh Samui's ring road is a single ride. Phuket is around 48 to 50 km long. Grab operates, which is the usual way people cover beach-to-beach.

Krabi and Ao Nang

Ao Nang is on the mainland rather than an island, and it has the most conventional service of any of these places: colour-coded fixed routes with flag-down stops, running every 10 to 20 minutes through the day, at 50 to 60 baht. That frequency is the outlier — elsewhere on this page the honest answer to "when does the next one come" is unknown, whereas here it is a number. Krabi Town to Ao Nang is about 17 to 20 km. Grab operates as well.

Koh Lanta

Fixed routes connect the west-coast beaches with Saladan town at the north end, at roughly 50 to 100 baht. The island is long and narrow, around 25 to 30 km, with the beaches strung along one coast. Operating hours are not reliably documented. Grab does not appear to operate.

Koh Phangan

Shared pickup trucks run along the main roads, but fares are frequently negotiated rather than posted, and reported prices vary widely — anywhere from 50 to 500 baht depending on distance and the negotiation. The island is about 16 to 18 km across, with accommodation spread across multiple separate bays. Operating hours are not documented. Grab does not operate.

Koh Chang

Shared trucks run along the west-coast main road and are flagged down; services tend to cluster around ferry arrival times. Fares run roughly 50 to 200 baht. Grab does not operate.

Koh Tao

Koh Tao is the outlier and worth describing carefully. Pickup trucks marked as taxis wait at Mae Haad pier, at the Sairee junction, and near the 7-Eleven in Chalok Baan Kao. They look like songthaews elsewhere. They do not behave like them.

Rates are fixed per route rather than per person: commonly 300 to 500 baht for one or two people from Mae Haad, with about 100 baht added for each additional passenger. Drivers frequently wait to fill the truck before departing, so a solo traveler either pays for the whole vehicle or waits for strangers. The island is small — about 7.5 km long, with the main bays generally under 5 km apart. Set that against Phuket, forty times the length, where the same journey distance costs 15 to 50 baht: the smallest island here has the highest per-trip fares, not the lowest. For two people the per-head cost falls by half; for four it falls again. The fare structure rewards groups and penalises solo travel, which is the reverse of how per-person fares work everywhere else on this page.

Mae Haad and the southern end of Sairee are walkable. The terrain between bays is hilly, and the roads have no footpaths. Grab does not operate.

Where Grab stops

The app-based option follows a clear line. Grab operates in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui and the Krabi and Ao Nang area. It does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan, and appears not to on Koh Lanta or Koh Chang.

That line falls in the same place as several other things. The islands without Grab are generally the ones where the shared-truck network is least formal, where fares are negotiated rather than posted, and where operating hours are least documented. The places with the most transport options have the most of all of them; the places with the fewest have fewer of each.

What is not documented

Two things are worth flagging as genuinely unclear rather than merely unstated. Songthaew operating hours on Koh Tao, Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta are not reliably published anywhere — the practical answer is daylight, with the evening cutoff varying. And Koh Phangan's fares are reported so inconsistently across sources that the honest description is a wide band rather than a figure.

Where fares are negotiated rather than posted, the price you are quoted and the price someone else was quoted may differ, and neither is wrong.

How this fits the rest of the trip

The transport picture on any one island is only half of what determines how you move around it. The other half is where the things you came for actually sit — how far the beach is from the town, whether the restaurants cluster in one strip or scatter across separate bays, and how far apart the bays are.

Those distances, and how they interact with each island's transport, are laid out in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

What is a songthaew?

A pickup truck with a covered bed and two bench seats, used as shared transport. On some islands it runs fixed routes and charges per person; on others the same vehicle operates as a chartered taxi at a fixed price for the whole truck.

Does Grab work on the Thai islands?

On some. It operates in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui and the Krabi and Ao Nang area, and does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan. Coverage on Koh Lanta and Koh Chang appears to be absent as well.

How much do songthaews cost?

It varies by island. Phuket runs about 15 to 50 baht, Krabi and Ao Nang 50 to 60, Koh Samui 30 to 150, Koh Lanta 50 to 100. Koh Tao is the outlier, with fixed per-route rates commonly 300 to 500 baht for one or two people.

What time do songthaews stop running?

Phuket runs roughly 6am to 6pm. Elsewhere the honest answer is daylight hours with an evening cutoff that is not reliably documented, particularly on Koh Tao, Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta.

Why are Koh Tao's taxi fares so high?

Rates there are fixed per route rather than per person, so a short trip costs the same whether you are one passenger or two. With the island only about 7.5 km long and the main bays under 5 km apart, the fares are high relative to the distances.

title: Where Grab Works in Thailand (and Where It Does Not)
excerpt: The ride-hailing coverage map, and what the islands without it use instead.
content:
Grab is Thailand's dominant ride-hailing app, and where it operates it removes most of the friction of getting around — fixed prices, no negotiation, no language barrier. Where it does not operate, the fallback is a different system with different rules. Here is the actual coverage map.

Where Grab operates

Grab runs in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui, and the Krabi and Ao Nang area. In each of these, both car and motorbike-taxi options are generally available, with the motorbike option cheaper and faster in traffic.

The pricing model is the thing that distinguishes it: you see the fare before you book, and it does not change. No meter to refuse, no negotiation, no route dispute.

Where it does not

Grab does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan. It appears not to operate on Koh Lanta or Koh Chang, though the evidence there is thinner.

The line falls in a consistent place. Grab covers the large developed islands and the mainland cities. It stops at the smaller islands.

What that line coincides with

The islands without Grab share several other characteristics, and they compound rather than offset.

Where Grab operates, the shared-truck networks also tend to be more formal — Phuket runs fixed routes 6am to 6pm at 15 to 50 baht, Ao Nang runs colour-coded routes every 10 to 20 minutes at 50 to 60 baht. Where Grab does not operate, fares are more often negotiated than posted, operating hours are less documented, and the per-trip cost is higher. The two do not offset each other. Somewhere with a good shared-truck network but no Grab would be one thing; somewhere with neither is another. The islands fall into the second group rather than the first.

Koh Tao is the clearest illustration. No Grab, and its pickup-truck taxis charge fixed per-route rates of about 300 to 500 baht for one or two people from Mae Haad, with roughly 100 baht per additional passenger, on an island only 7.5 km long. Koh Phangan has no Grab and fares reported anywhere between 50 and 500 baht depending on distance and negotiation.

So the places with the fewest transport options also have the least price transparency and the highest per-trip cost. The gap is not evenly distributed — and it runs opposite to what island size would suggest, since the small islands people expect to be cheap and simple are the ones where a single trip costs the most and the price is least knowable in advance. On Phuket or Samui the choice is between several priced options; on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan it is between one unpriced option and your own two wheels.

The metered alternative in the cities

In Bangkok and Chiang Mai, metered taxis operate alongside Grab. The meter exists and is legally required to be used. Whether a given driver uses it is a separate matter, which is covered in our guide to tuk-tuks and taxis in Thailand.

The practical difference is that Grab's price is agreed before the ride and a taxi's is settled after it. That distinction matters more where you do not speak the language or know the route.

What is not well documented

Wait times are the main gap. There is no reliable figure for how long a Grab typically takes to arrive in any of the places it operates, and reported experiences vary with time of day and location within each place.

Coverage on Koh Lanta and Koh Chang is also less certain than the clear absence on Koh Tao and Koh Phangan — the evidence points to no service, but it rests on fewer sources.

How coverage interacts with everything else

Ride-hailing availability is one layer of a picture that also includes how far apart things sit on each island, what the shared-truck networks cost and when they run, and what the road conditions are like after dark. Each of those is documented separately and none of them alone describes what a day of moving around actually looks like.

How the layers combine for a specific set of bases is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Does Grab work in Thailand?

In Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui and the Krabi and Ao Nang area. It does not operate on Koh Tao or Koh Phangan, and appears not to on Koh Lanta or Koh Chang.

What do I use where Grab does not operate?

The local shared pickup trucks, which on those islands tend to run as fixed-rate charter taxis rather than shared routes. On Koh Tao that means about 300 to 500 baht per trip for one or two people.

Is Grab cheaper than a taxi in Bangkok?

Not necessarily cheaper, but the price is fixed and shown before you book, which removes the meter question entirely.

Does Grab offer motorbike taxis?

Yes, in the areas where it operates. The motorbike option is cheaper than the car option and faster in heavy traffic.

How long do Grab rides take to arrive?

There is no reliable published figure. Reported wait times vary considerably by time of day and by location within each area it serves.

title: Is Grab Safe and Worth It in Thailand?
excerpt: Grab is Thailand's dominant ride-hailing app — here's how it works, whether it's safe and worth it, where it does and doesn't operate well, and tips for using it.
content:
Grab is the Uber of Southeast Asia, and in Thailand it's one of the most useful apps a traveler can have. It handles rides, food delivery, and more, all with upfront pricing and cashless payment. But it doesn't work equally well everywhere in the country, and there are a few things worth knowing before you rely on it. Here's the full picture.

What is Grab and how does it work?

Grab is a super-app: you use it to book cars, taxis, and motorbike taxis, order food, and even send packages. For getting around, you enter your destination, see the price and the driver before you book, and pay either in cash or by a card linked to the app. It works just like Uber or Lyft, which makes it instantly familiar to American travelers. Download it and set it up before your trip while you're still on home Wi-Fi. Setting up an account in advance — verifying your phone number and adding a payment method — means you can hail a ride the moment you land rather than fumbling with the app on airport WiFi after a long flight.

Is Grab safe?

Yes — Grab is generally very safe and is the option many travelers feel most comfortable with, precisely because everything is tracked and transparent. You can see the driver's name, vehicle, and rating, the route is logged in the app, the fare is fixed in advance so there's no meter scam, and you can share your trip with someone. For solo travelers and anyone wary of negotiating with taxis or tuk-tuks, Grab removes most of the friction and uncertainty.

Is it worth it?

For convenience and peace of mind, absolutely. The upfront pricing alone is worth it — you avoid the haggling and the inflated "tourist" fares that come with flagging down tuk-tuks or non-metered taxis. It's especially valuable when you're tired, loaded with luggage, going somewhere off the train lines, or out late. In Bangkok, a metered taxi can occasionally be cheaper, but the certainty and ease of Grab usually win.

Where Grab works well — and where it doesn't

Grab works excellently in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, and most cities. Coverage is more limited on some islands and in resort areas, where local taxi cartels have resisted ride-hailing — Phuket is the notorious example, with limited Grab availability and sometimes tension around it, and parts of Krabi and Samui can be patchy too. In these places you may wait longer, pay more, or need to use local taxis and songthaews instead. Don't assume Grab will be instantly available everywhere the way it is in Bangkok.

Grab for food and more

Grab isn't just for rides — GrabFood is a hugely popular food-delivery service that's perfect for a night in, a meal when you're jet-lagged, or simply trying local restaurants without going out. It works just like the ride service: browse nearby restaurants, order, track the delivery, and pay in the app. For travelers staying in an apartment or recovering from a long flight, it's a genuinely useful way to eat well cheaply. The app also handles package delivery and other services, though rides and food are what most visitors use.

Tips for using Grab in Thailand

Set it up before you travel and add a payment card if you'd rather not use cash. Choose your pickup point carefully — a clear landmark or hotel entrance avoids confusion, since not all drivers speak English. Use the in-app chat's translation if needed. Have cash as backup for cash trips and for places where Grab is thin. And check the car type — GrabCar for comfort, GrabTaxi to hail a metered taxi through the app, or a motorbike option for quick solo hops through traffic. Fares are low overall; check a live converter rather than a fixed figure:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

FAQ

Is Grab safe to use in Thailand?

Yes — it's one of the safest ways to get around. The driver, vehicle, route, and fixed fare are all shown in the app, with no meter scams or haggling, which many travelers find reassuring.

Is Grab cheaper than taxis in Thailand?

Often comparable, and the upfront fixed price means no inflated tourist fares. In Bangkok a metered taxi can occasionally be cheaper, but Grab's certainty and ease usually make it worth it.

Does Grab work everywhere in Thailand?

It works great in Bangkok, Chiang Mai, and most cities, but is limited on some islands and resort areas — Phuket especially, where local taxis have resisted it. Have local taxis or songthaews as backup there.

Do I need cash if I use Grab?

You can link a card and pay cashless, but carry cash as backup — for cash-fare trips and for islands or areas where Grab availability is thin and you'll need local transport.

title: Renting a Car in Thailand: Paperwork, Cost and Roads
excerpt: The four-wheel alternative — what the licence rules require, what the insurance covers, and where the roads suit it.
content:
Renting a car gets far less attention than renting a scooter, and the requirements are meaningfully different. Here is what a car actually involves in Thailand — the paperwork, the cost, the roads it suits, and what the insurance does and does not cover.

What the paperwork requires

Driving a car in Thailand requires a valid home driving licence plus an International Driving Permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention. In the United States, AAA and AATA are the only authorised issuers, at around $20, available same-day in person at a AAA branch.

There is a difference here that catches people who have read about scooters. A car requires the ordinary driving licence an American already holds. A motorbike requires a motorcycle endorsement on that licence, which most Americans do not have, and which an IDP does not add. The permit that covers you for a car may not cover you for a scooter — the entitlement comes from the home licence, and the IDP only translates it.

What it costs

Daily rates run roughly 700 to 1,500 baht depending on class, with economy cars at the lower end and SUVs and pickups higher. That sits well above a day of songthaew trips almost anywhere except Koh Tao, where four fixed-rate taxi runs at 300 to 500 baht each would cost more than a car for the day — if a car were practical on an island that size, which it is not. Rates move with season and demand, so treat any figure as a shape rather than a price:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

What the insurance covers

A standard rental includes compulsory third-party liability, which covers injury or death to other people. It does not cover damage to the rental vehicle itself.

Collision damage waiver and theft protection are separate add-ons, and both carry common exclusions — off-road driving being the usual one. The gap between "insured" as the counter describes it and "insured" as a renter assumes it tends to sit exactly there: third-party injury is covered by default, the car you are driving is not.

Worth reading the specific terms rather than the summary, and worth checking what your own travel insurance says about rental vehicles, since policies differ on whether they duplicate or supplement the rental company's cover.

Where the roads suit a car

Road networks vary enough that the question is less about preference than about physical fit.

The mainland and the north have the road networks best suited to a car. Chiang Mai and the routes north of it are mountainous with sharp curves and switchbacks — Route 1095 to Pai is commonly cited as having 762 curves over about 135 km — but they are proper roads with room for four wheels.

Phuket and Koh Samui both have developed road networks. Samui's ring road runs about 51 km around the island; Phuket is 48 to 50 km long with winding coastal and mountain roads and heavier traffic than the smaller islands.

The smaller islands have narrow roads that do not accommodate cars well. Koh Tao is about 7.5 km long with one main paved road between the villages and side roads over hilly terrain to the east coast bays. Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta are similarly constrained. This is where the paperwork advantage inverts: a car is the easier vehicle to be licensed for and the harder one to actually use, whereas a scooter is the harder one to be licensed for and fits everywhere. The places where the licensing question is most awkward are the places where four wheels are least practical.

Parking

Resorts and shopping centres generally provide parking. The busy beach towns are constrained, and street parking is restricted to legal zones.

Night driving

Street lighting is poor to absent outside Bangkok and the main urban areas. Island and mountain roads are largely unlit after dark, which is the single most consistent road-condition finding across every region. The mountain routes that make a car attractive during the day are the ones with no lighting at night.

How this sits beside the alternatives

A car is one of four ways to cover ground in Thailand, alongside a scooter, the shared-truck networks, and app-based rides where they operate. Each has a different paperwork requirement, a different cost structure, and a different set of places it physically fits.

Which combination suits a particular set of bases and a particular tolerance for driving is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Do I need an International Driving Permit to rent a car in Thailand?

Yes — a valid home licence plus a 1949 Geneva Convention IDP. In the US, AAA and AATA are the only authorised issuers, at around $20, available same day in person.

Is a car easier than a scooter, paperwork-wise?

For most Americans, yes. A car requires the ordinary driving licence you already hold. A motorbike requires a motorcycle endorsement that most US licences lack, and an IDP does not add one.

What does rental car insurance in Thailand cover?

Standard rentals include compulsory third-party liability, covering injury to other people. Damage to the rental vehicle itself is not included — collision damage waiver and theft protection are separate add-ons with common exclusions.

How much does a rental car cost in Thailand?

Roughly 700 to 1,500 baht per day depending on class, though rates move with season and demand.

Where in Thailand do the roads suit a rental car?

The mainland, the north, Phuket and Koh Samui have developed road networks. The smaller islands — Koh Tao, Koh Phangan, Koh Lanta — have narrow roads that accommodate cars poorly.

title: Tuk-Tuks, Taxis, and Songthaews: Getting Around Thai Towns
excerpt: How to use Thailand's local transport — tuk-tuks, taxis, songthaews, and motorbike taxis — how each works, how to avoid being overcharged, and when to use which.
content:
Beyond the apps and the Skytrain, Thailand has a colorful array of local transport — three-wheeled tuk-tuks, shared songthaew trucks, metered taxis, and motorbike taxis. Knowing how each works, and how to avoid being overcharged, makes getting around Thai towns easy and even fun. Here's your guide to the local rides.

Tuk-tuks

The iconic three-wheeled tuk-tuk is a quintessential Thai experience — open-air, zippy, and fun for a short ride. But manage expectations: they are not cheaper than a metered taxi or Grab, the price is always negotiated (there's no meter), and tourist fares are often inflated. In Bangkok especially, some tuk-tuk drivers run the "gem shop" scam, offering a suspiciously cheap fare in exchange for stopping at shops where they earn commission. Agree the price before you get in, keep it to short hops, and treat tuk-tuks as an occasional novelty rather than your main transport.

Taxis

Metered taxis are plentiful in Bangkok and other cities, and cheap if the driver uses the meter. The rule: insist on "meter" and decline drivers who quote a flat fare instead (which is usually inflated). Most taxis are honest, but the meter refusal is a common tourist hassle. Outside the big cities, metered taxis are less common, and you'll rely more on songthaews and other options. Using Grab to book a taxi removes the haggling.

Songthaews

The workhorses of many Thai towns, songthaews ("two rows," named for the bench seats in the back) are shared pickup trucks that function as informal buses or shared taxis. In cities like Chiang Mai, the red songthaews run flexible routes — you flag one down, tell the driver your destination, and pay a small flat fare per person, sharing with others heading the same way. They're cheap, ubiquitous, and a local way to get around. In some towns they run fixed routes; in others they act more like shared taxis you negotiate.

Motorbike taxis

For beating traffic on short trips, motorbike taxis — drivers in colored numbered vests, often clustered at corners and intersections — are fast and cheap. You hop on the back and they weave through jams that would gridlock a car. They're great for a quick solo hop if you're comfortable on a bike (you'll usually get a helmet). Agree the fare first. They're a common local choice for short distances, especially in congested Bangkok.

How to avoid being overcharged

A few habits keep fares fair: agree the price before getting in for any negotiated ride (tuk-tuk, motorbike taxi, non-metered situations); insist on the meter in taxis; know the rough going rate by asking your hotel; use Grab when you want a fixed, transparent price with no haggling; and have small notes ready so "no change" can't inflate your fare. A friendly, confident manner helps — drivers are quicker to quote fair prices to travelers who seem to know the score.

How local transport varies by destination

The mix you'll use changes depending on where you are. In Bangkok, you have the full range plus the Skytrain and metro, so tuk-tuks and motorbike taxis are mostly for novelty or beating jams. In Chiang Mai, the red songthaews are the everyday workhorse and Grab works well. On the islands and in resort towns, songthaews and rented scooters dominate, taxis can be pricey, and Grab availability is patchy (notoriously so in Phuket). In smaller towns, songthaews and motorbike taxis may be your only options. Knowing the local norm — easily checked by asking your hotel — saves both money and confusion when you arrive somewhere new.

Which should you use when?

The practical playbook: use Grab or metered taxis for comfort, fixed prices, and longer trips; songthaews for cheap local hops and the authentic experience; motorbike taxis to beat traffic on quick solo trips; and tuk-tuks when you want the fun of the experience and don't mind paying a bit for it. Mixing them as suits each trip is part of the rhythm of getting around Thailand. Fares are low across the board; check a live converter rather than a fixed figure:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

FAQ

Are tuk-tuks cheaper than taxis in Thailand?

No — tuk-tuks are usually not cheaper than a metered taxi or Grab, and the fare is always negotiated (often inflated for tourists). Treat them as a fun occasional experience and agree the price before getting in.

What is a songthaew?

A shared pickup truck with bench seats that works as an informal bus or shared taxi. In cities like Chiang Mai, you flag one down, state your destination, and pay a small flat fare per person — cheap and very local.

How do I avoid being overcharged by taxis?

Insist on the meter and decline drivers who quote a flat fare. Better still, use Grab for a fixed, transparent price with no haggling. Knowing the rough going rate (ask your hotel) also helps.

Are motorbike taxis safe?

They're a fast, cheap way to beat traffic on short hops, used widely by locals, and you'll usually get a helmet. They carry the inherent risks of motorbikes, so they suit confident riders comfortable on the back of a bike.

title: How to Get from Bangkok to Phuket, Krabi, and Koh Samui
excerpt: The best route from Bangkok to each major island: just fly to Phuket and Krabi, and choose between a direct Samui flight or the cheaper Surat-Thani-plus-ferry route for Koh Samui.
content:
Once you've done Bangkok, the big logistical question is how to reach the southern islands. The three most popular destinations — Phuket, Krabi, and Koh Samui — each have a best route from the capital, and they're not all the same. Here's exactly how to get to each, with the fast way, the cheap way, and which to choose.

Bangkok to Phuket

The fast way (recommended): fly. Phuket has its own international airport (HKT), and the flight from Bangkok takes about 1 hour 25 minutes. Both Bangkok airports serve it, with frequent budget and full-service flights. From Phuket airport it's a 30-minute-to-one-hour taxi to most beaches. For almost everyone, flying is the clear choice.

The slow/cheap way: overland by bus or train to the south plus a road connection — a long journey (often overnight) that only makes sense if you're specifically avoiding flying or stopping somewhere en route.

Bangkok to Krabi

Fly. Krabi also has its own airport (KBV), about 1 hour 25 minutes from Bangkok, and it's the gateway to Ao Nang, Railay, and the Andaman islands. From the airport it's roughly 30–45 minutes to Ao Nang. As with Phuket, flying is the sensible default; the overland alternative is long.

If you're deciding between Phuket and Krabi as a destination, both are easy to reach — the choice is about the place, not the journey (Krabi for dramatic cliffs and a calmer scene, Phuket for more resorts and nightlife).

Bangkok to Koh Samui

Koh Samui is an island, so reaching it always ends with either a flight or a ferry — and this is where the routes genuinely differ:

The fast way: fly direct to Samui (USM). The flight is about 1 hour, but Samui's airport is privately operated (by Bangkok Airways) and fares run higher than to other islands. It's the quickest, most comfortable option.

The cheaper way: fly to Surat Thani, then ferry. Fly Bangkok → Surat Thani (on the mainland), then take a bus-and-ferry or combined ticket across to Koh Samui. It's noticeably cheaper than flying direct to Samui, at the cost of a few extra hours and a transfer.

The budget way: train or bus plus ferry. An overnight train or bus from Bangkok to Surat Thani, then the ferry — slow but inexpensive, and the overnight leg saves a hotel night.

How long does the whole journey really take?

The flight time is only part of the door-to-door picture, and it's worth planning around. To Phuket or Krabi, budget roughly half a day total: time to the Bangkok airport, the 1h25 flight, and 30–60 minutes from the island airport to your beach. To Koh Samui direct, similar — about an hour in the air plus transfers. The Surat Thani-plus-ferry route to Samui is the long one: the flight is short, but the airport-to-pier transfer and the ferry crossing add several hours, so treat it as most of a travel day.

The practical takeaway: if you're flying to an island on the same day you arrive internationally in Bangkok, give yourself a generous connection — especially if your domestic flight leaves from the other Bangkok airport — or simply overnight in Bangkok and fly south fresh the next morning.

Which route should you choose?

For Phuket and Krabi, just fly — it's cheap, fast, and obvious. For Koh Samui, fly direct if you value time and comfort and don't mind paying more; fly to Surat Thani and ferry across if you'd rather save money. Whichever island, book domestic flights a week or two ahead for the best fares, and check which Bangkok airport your flight departs from.

One season note: ferry crossings to the Gulf islands can be rough or disrupted during the wettest months (around October–December for the Gulf), so build in buffer time if you're traveling then. Fares move, so check current prices and convert with a live tool:

FAQ

What's the fastest way from Bangkok to the islands?

Fly. Phuket and Krabi are about 1h25 from Bangkok and have their own airports; Koh Samui is about 1 hour direct. Flying beats the long overland routes for all three.

Is it cheaper to fly to Koh Samui or take a ferry?

Flying direct to Samui is fastest but pricier (its airport is privately run). Flying to Surat Thani and taking a bus-and-ferry across is noticeably cheaper, at the cost of a few extra hours.

Do I need to fly into Phuket, or can I go overland?

You can go overland by bus or train plus a road connection, but it's a long, often overnight journey. Flying (about 1h25) is far easier and usually inexpensive.

Should I worry about ferries in the rainy season?

Crossings to the Gulf islands (Samui, Phangan, Tao) can be rough or disrupted during their wettest months around October–December. Build in buffer time and check conditions if traveling then.

title: Thailand's Ferries: How to Get to the Islands
excerpt: How Thailand's island ferries work — the main routes to the Andaman and Gulf islands, types of boats, how to book, and tips for a smooth crossing.
content:
Almost every Thai island trip involves a boat at some point, and understanding how the ferry system works makes island travel far smoother. From big car ferries to fast speedboats and combined bus-and-boat tickets, here's how to get out to Thailand's islands and what to expect on the way.

The two coasts and their islands

Thailand's islands split between two coasts, each with its own ferry hubs. On the Andaman coast (west), boats leave from Phuket and Krabi-area piers for Phi Phi, the Hong Islands, Koh Lanta, and beyond. On the Gulf coast (east), the main gateway is around Surat Thani and the Donsak pier, serving Koh Samui, Koh Phangan, and Koh Tao. Remember the coasts have opposite seasons, so the smoothest crossings depend on traveling each coast in its drier months. Crossing from one coast's islands to the other's mid-trip means returning to the mainland and a long overland transfer, so it's almost always better to pick one coast and explore its islands rather than trying to combine both.

Types of boats

Large ferries are the workhorses — slower but stable and affordable, carrying passengers (and sometimes vehicles) on the main routes like Surat Thani to Koh Samui. Speedboats are faster and pricier, ideal for shorter hops and day trips, though bumpier in rough seas. Longtail boats handle short local transfers, like Ao Nang to Railay. Catamarans run some popular routes, balancing speed and comfort. Which you take depends on the route and how much you value speed over cost. On many popular routes you'll have a choice between a cheaper, slower ferry and a faster, pricier speedboat covering the same crossing — worth weighing against the sea conditions, since speedboats are far less comfortable than big ferries when the water is choppy.

Combined tickets make it easy

The most convenient way to reach many islands is a combined ticket that bundles the whole journey — typically a flight-plus-ferry or bus/van-plus-ferry — on one booking. For example, you can buy a single ticket from Bangkok to Koh Samui that covers the flight to Surat Thani, the transfer to the pier, and the ferry across. These take the guesswork out of connections and are widely sold by ferry operators and travel agents. For first-timers especially, they're worth the small premium.

How to book

You can book ferries in advance online through ferry operators or booking platforms, or buy tickets locally at piers and travel agents once you're there. In peak season (and for popular routes), booking ahead secures your spot and saves queuing. For day trips to islands like Phi Phi, booking a tour the day before is standard. Off-season and for flexible travelers, buying at the pier usually works fine.

How long do crossings take?

Crossing times vary widely by route and boat. Short hops like Ao Nang to Railay take 10–15 minutes by longtail; Phuket or Krabi to Phi Phi runs roughly 1.5–2 hours by ferry (less by speedboat); and Surat Thani area to Koh Samui is around 1.5–2 hours on the big ferries. Day trips out to island clusters can involve an hour or more each way. None are marathon journeys, but factor them into your arrival and departure days — and remember that a "quick" island can still mean a half-day of travel once you add transfers to and from the piers at each end.

Tips for a smooth crossing

Travel light and keep valuables accessible — you'll load bags on and off boats, sometimes wading a little. Take motion-sickness tablets before you board if you're prone to it, as crossings can be choppy. Choose daytime crossings so you don't lose beach time and can see the scenery. Build in buffer time around weather, especially in the wetter months when rough seas can delay or cancel boats. And protect electronics from spray with a dry bag on speedboats and longtails. FAQ

How do I get to the Thai islands?

By ferry, speedboat, or longtail boat from mainland piers — often via combined flight-plus-ferry or bus-plus-ferry tickets that cover the whole journey on one booking. The Andaman and Gulf coasts have separate ferry hubs.

Should I book ferries in advance?

In peak season and for popular routes, yes — it secures your spot and saves queuing. Off-season or for flexible travel, buying at the pier or through a local agent usually works fine.

Are combined bus-and-ferry tickets worth it?

For most travelers, yes — they bundle the whole journey (flight or bus plus transfer plus ferry) onto one booking, removing the hassle of arranging connections yourself. Worth the small premium.

Can ferries be cancelled by weather?

Yes, especially in the wetter months when seas get rough. Build buffer time into your plans around island crossings, and don't schedule a tight onward connection right after a ferry in bad-weather season.

title: When Thai Ferries Cancel: What Actually Happens
excerpt: Who decides when a crossing is suspended, what happens to your ticket, and which islands let you fly out instead.
content:
Ferries to Thailand's islands get cancelled. Not often, and not everywhere — but when a crossing is suspended, most travelers discover they have no idea what happens next: whether the ticket is refunded, whether they can fly instead, or who is responsible for the connection waiting at the other end. Here is how cancellation actually works, and which of those questions has a good answer.

Who decides

Operators make the call on their own sailings, guided by Marine Department weather warnings and their own assessment of conditions at the pier. The Marine Department — the government body under the Ministry of Transport that oversees maritime safety — can also order suspensions outright.

The practical point is that nobody at your hotel, and no travel agent, can tell you in advance whether tomorrow's boat will run. It is a decision made close to departure by people looking at the sea, and it is not negotiable when it goes against you.

Which crossings are most exposed

Rough conditions do not affect all routes equally. Crossings to Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are the ones most frequently suspended, partly because of the open water involved and partly because of the boats that serve them. The two coasts also have opposite wet seasons, so exposure moves around the calendar rather than applying to the whole country at once — the Gulf islands are most affected roughly October to December, the Andaman side around September and October.

Boat type matters too. Speedboats stop running in conditions that larger ferries will still cross in, so the fast option is also the fragile one.

What happens to your ticket

Booked directly with the operator

Weather cancellations commonly result in a rebooking or a credit rather than a cash refund, and the specifics vary by operator — some tickets are sold non-refundable outright, cancellation or not. This surprises people who expect a weather cancellation to mean their money back. Contractually, it usually means a seat on a later boat.

Where a speedboat is cancelled, the normal outcome is that you are moved onto the same company's slower ferry rather than refunded the difference in price. You paid for speed and you get the crossing.

Combined bus-and-boat or flight-and-boat tickets

This is the one worth understanding before you buy. Combined tickets are convenient and widely sold, and when only the boat leg fails, the onward bus or flight portion is often not covered — the responsibility depends on who sold you the ticket and what their terms say about partial failure.

It is worth reading those terms at the point of purchase rather than at the pier. A ticket that bundles three legs is not automatically a ticket that protects three legs.

Booked through a platform

Aggregator bookings generally follow the underlying operator's policy, with the platform's own cancellation window layered on top. The extra intermediary means an extra link in the chain when you need to reach someone quickly.

Whether you can fly instead

This is the most useful thing to know before you choose an island, and it is entirely knowable in advance. Some islands have an airport. Some do not, and the boat is the only way off.

Air escape availableBoat only
Koh Samui (USM)Koh Tao
Phuket (HKT)Koh Phangan
Krabi (KBV)Koh Lanta

Read those two columns together with the previous section and the shape of the problem appears: Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are both the most cancellation-prone crossings and the islands with no way out except a boat. When a suspension hits, travelers on Samui have options. Travelers on Koh Tao have a wait.

The connection at the other end

Here is the fact most travelers have backwards: a separately booked domestic flight is not protected by your international ticket. If you booked your Bangkok-to-island flight yourself, on a different reservation from the long-haul home, the airline that flies you across the Pacific has no obligation to you when a boat makes you miss it. There is no rebooking, no protection, no through-checking. You buy a new ticket.

Most people assume some invisible safety net exists because their legs are all part of one trip. It does not exist. Two separate bookings are two separate contracts, and weather is nobody's fault, which means it is yours.

Trip interruption cover is the part of a policy that speaks to this, rather than the medical cover most policies lead with — worth checking what your travel insurance says about missed connections caused by weather before you need to find out.

Booking around it

Some things are simply in your control:

  • Take the earlier crossing. If a day's sailings are going to be cancelled, the later ones are likelier to go first, and an early boat leaves room to recover the same day.
  • Prefer the larger ferry when conditions look marginal. It is slower and it crosses in weather that grounds the speedboats.
  • Book the boat leg directly with the operator when that leg is carrying something important, so there is one fewer party between you and the rebooking.
  • Know before you go whether your island has an airport. That single fact determines whether a suspension is an inconvenience or a genuine problem.

Ferry fares vary by route, boat type and season, so check a live figure rather than planning against a fixed one:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

Where this decision actually sits

Notice what happened across all of this: almost none of it is really about boats. Which island you can reach, whether it has an airport, which coast you are on in which month, and how your flights are booked are four separate decisions that people make weeks apart — and they only fail together. The travelers who get caught are rarely the ones who picked the wrong ferry. They are the ones whose island, month and departure arrangements were each individually reasonable.

Working out how those four fit together for a specific set of dates is the kind of thing that is easier to read once than to reconstruct from a dozen separate pages, and it is worked out in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

Who decides whether a Thai ferry is cancelled?

The operator makes the call on its own sailings, guided by Marine Department weather warnings and conditions at the pier. The Marine Department can also order suspensions directly. It is decided close to departure, not days ahead.

Do I get a refund if my ferry is cancelled?

Usually not in cash. Weather cancellations commonly result in a rebooking or credit, policies vary by operator, and some tickets are non-refundable regardless. Combined bus-and-boat tickets are the ones to check carefully, since a failed boat leg often does not cover the onward portion.

Which Thai island crossings are cancelled most often?

Crossings to Koh Tao and Koh Phangan are the most frequently suspended. Speedboats stop running in conditions that larger ferries still cross in, so the fast option is the more fragile one.

Can I fly instead if the ferry is cancelled?

Only from islands with an airport — Koh Samui, Phuket and Krabi have one. Koh Tao, Koh Phangan and Koh Lanta do not, so the boat is the only way off.

Will my airline rebook me if a ferry makes me miss my flight?

Not if the flights were booked separately. A separately booked domestic leg has no protection from your international ticket — you would be buying a new one. Trip interruption cover on a travel insurance policy is the thing that speaks to this.

title: Bangkok Has Two Airports: The Transfer Between Them
excerpt: About 50 km apart, 45 minutes to 2.5 hours by road, no rail link, and no official minimum connection time.
content:
Bangkok has two airports about 50 km apart, and travellers routinely book an international arrival at one and a domestic departure from the other without noticing. Here is what moving between them actually involves.

Which airport is which

Suvarnabhumi (BKK) handles full-service and most international carriers. If you are flying in from the United States, this is almost certainly where you land.

Don Mueang (DMK) handles primarily low-cost carriers, including a large share of the domestic network. If you booked a cheap flight to Phuket or Chiang Mai separately, there is a good chance it leaves from here.

They are separate airports roughly 50 km apart by road, not two terminals of the same place.

How long the transfer takes

Off-peak, the road transfer runs 45 to 60 minutes. In Bangkok traffic it runs 90 minutes to two and a half hours.

That spread is the fact worth carrying. The same journey can take three times as long depending on the hour, and the hour is set by when your inbound flight lands rather than by anything you choose.

There is no rail link between them

The Airport Rail Link connects Suvarnabhumi to the city. It does not reach Don Mueang. Any transfer between the two airports is a road journey and is subject to road conditions.

The free shuttle, and who cannot use it

Airports of Thailand runs a free shuttle bus between the two airports, roughly 05:00 to midnight, taking around 50 minutes in normal traffic.

The eligibility rule is stricter than it first appears. The service is exclusively for passengers transferring between the two airports — a boarding pass or e-ticket for an onward flight and a passport must be shown at the counter. The airport authority states plainly that non-connecting passengers and the general public are not eligible.

So someone spending a night in the city between two flights is not a transferring passenger by this definition, and pays for their own transport in both directions.

Where it goes from

At Suvarnabhumi, the shuttle leaves from Level 2 (arrivals), Gate 3, where a desk checks flight details. At Don Mueang, the shuttle counter sits inside the terminal near exit 6, and check-in there happens before going out to the stop.

What an international-to-domestic connection involves

None of this happens airside. An arriving international passenger:

  • Clears immigration
  • Reclaims checked baggage
  • Exits to landside
  • Travels 50 km across Bangkok
  • Checks in again from scratch at the other airport

It is a complete re-entry into the system, not a transfer within one. Bags are not through-checked between separately booked tickets, which is the mechanical reason each step has to be repeated.

No official minimum connection time

Airlines publish minimum connection times for connections within an airport. For a connection between Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang, no official minimum is published at all.

That absence is itself the fact. Various figures circulate in guides and forums, and none of them carries any authority — there is no airport or airline standard being cited. What exists instead is the arithmetic above: immigration, baggage, a road journey that varies between 45 minutes and 2.5 hours, and a fresh check-in.

Where this decision actually gets made

Almost nobody chooses this transfer deliberately. It arrives as a consequence — the international ticket was booked for price and schedule, the domestic leg was booked separately weeks later, and the two airports were never the same field in either search.

How the airport split interacts with the rest of an itinerary is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

How far apart are Bangkok's two airports?

About 50 km by road. Suvarnabhumi (BKK) handles international and full-service carriers; Don Mueang (DMK) handles primarily low-cost and domestic flights.

How long does the BKK to DMK transfer take?

45 to 60 minutes off-peak, and 90 minutes to two and a half hours in traffic.

Is there a free shuttle between Bangkok's airports?

Yes, run by Airports of Thailand, roughly 05:00 to midnight. It is exclusively for passengers transferring between the two airports — a boarding pass for an onward flight and a passport are required, and non-connecting passengers are not eligible.

Can I take a train between the two airports?

No. The Airport Rail Link serves Suvarnabhumi and the city but does not reach Don Mueang, so any transfer is a road journey.

What is the minimum connection time between BKK and DMK?

There is no official published minimum. What exists is the process: immigration, baggage reclaim, a road transfer of 45 minutes to 2.5 hours, and a fresh check-in.

title: Domestic Flights in Thailand: Airlines, Routes, and Booking Tips
excerpt: Domestic flights are how you link Thailand's far-apart regions cheaply and fast. The airlines, the Bangkok two-airport trap, the most useful routes, and how to book them well.
content:
Domestic flights are the secret to a good Thailand itinerary. The country is large — driving or training between Bangkok, the north, and the southern islands eats whole days — but a flight covers the same distance in an hour or two for not much money. If you're combining regions on a short trip, flying is almost always the right move. Here's how Thailand's domestic flight network works and how to book it well.

The main airlines

Thailand has a competitive domestic market, which keeps fares low. The main carriers you'll see:

Budget airlines: Thai AirAsia, Thai Lion Air, Nok Air, and Thai Vietjet run the bulk of domestic routes at low base fares (with extra charges for bags and seats, as budget airlines do everywhere).

Full-service: Bangkok Airways (which owns and exclusively serves Samui airport) and Thai Airways, the national carrier, offer a more comfortable experience at higher prices.

Bangkok's two airports — don't mix them up

This catches people out: Bangkok has two airports. Suvarnabhumi (BKK) handles most full-service and international flights; Don Mueang (DMK) is the budget-airline hub. When you book a domestic flight, check which airport it departs from — if you're connecting from an international arrival, you may need to transfer between the two, which takes an hour or more across the city. Leave plenty of time, or book your domestic leg from the same airport you land at where possible.

The most useful routes

For a typical first trip, these are the flights that save the most time:

Bangkok ↔ Chiang Mai (about 1h15) — the north. Far better than the 10–12 hour overland trip.

Bangkok ↔ Phuket (about 1h25) — the Andaman coast.

Bangkok ↔ Krabi (about 1h25) — the other Andaman gateway.

Bangkok ↔ Koh Samui (about 1h) — the Gulf coast, served by Bangkok Airways.

There are also useful direct routes that skip Bangkok, such as Chiang Mai to Phuket, which save a backtrack when you're moving from the north straight to the south.

What about luggage and small airports?

Budget-airline fares usually include only a small carry-on, so add checked baggage when you book (it's cheaper online than at the counter) and weigh your bags — Thai budget carriers enforce limits strictly. The island airports are small and can get congested in peak season, so arrive with a comfortable buffer. Samui's airport, run by Bangkok Airways, is unusually pleasant — an open-air, garden-style terminal — but its flights are pricier than the budget norm.

Is flying always the right call?

For linking distant regions on a trip of two weeks or less, almost always yes — the time saved is enormous. The exception is when the journey itself is the experience: the overnight sleeper train from Bangkok to Chiang Mai is a genuinely enjoyable, scenic ride that also saves a hotel night. On a longer, slower trip, mixing in one or two train or bus legs for the scenery can be worth it. But for getting to the islands quickly, fly.

How to book well

Book a week or two ahead. Fares are cheapest in advance and climb close to departure, especially in peak season (November–February).

Compare across airlines. A flight-comparison search shows all the budget and full-service options side by side; the cheapest carrier varies by route and date.

Read the baggage rules. Budget fares often include only a small carry-on; add checked bags during booking, where they're cheaper than at the airport.

Factor airport transfers. A "cheap" flight from the far Bangkok airport can cost you the savings in a cross-city taxi and lost time.

Book directly or through a comparison tool. A flight-comparison search is the easiest way to see every airline at once, and you can either book through it or go to the airline's own site once you've found the route and price you want. Either works; the comparison step is what saves you money, because the cheapest carrier genuinely changes from route to route and day to day.

Fares move constantly, so check current prices rather than trusting any fixed figure, and translate baht with a live converter:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

FAQ

Are domestic flights in Thailand cheap?

Generally yes — a competitive market with several budget airlines keeps base fares low, especially booked a week or two ahead. Watch for extra charges on bags and seat selection.

Which airlines fly domestically in Thailand?

Budget carriers Thai AirAsia, Thai Lion Air, Nok Air, and Thai Vietjet, plus full-service Bangkok Airways (which serves Koh Samui) and Thai Airways.

Why does Bangkok have two airports?

Suvarnabhumi (BKK) handles most international and full-service flights; Don Mueang (DMK) is the budget-airline hub. Check which one your domestic flight uses — transferring between them takes over an hour.

Should I fly or take the train between Thai cities?

Fly if your time is limited — a flight is 1–1.5 hours versus 10+ hours overland. The overnight train to Chiang Mai is a lovely experience if you have time to spare, but flying wins for short trips.

title: Domestic Flight or Overnight Train in Thailand
excerpt: An hour in the air against thirteen in a berth — and what each does to the day around it.
content:
Bangkok to Chiang Mai, or Bangkok toward the southern islands, can be covered by air in about an hour or by sleeper train overnight. They are not the same journey in any respect except the endpoints. Here is what each involves.

The flight

Bangkok to Chiang Mai takes about an hour in the air. Bangkok to Phuket runs about an hour and fifteen minutes; to Koh Samui about an hour.

Domestic routes are operated by Thai Airways, Bangkok Airways, Thai AirAsia, Nok Air and Thai Lion Air. Which airport a flight leaves from depends on the carrier — the low-cost airlines operate largely from Don Mueang, the full-service ones from Suvarnabhumi, and those are two separate airports about 50 km apart.

The hour in the air is not the journey. Airport travel at both ends, check-in, security and baggage reclaim surround it, and where the departure airport is not the one you arrived into, a 50 km road transfer surrounds that.

The overnight train

Sleepers run north to Chiang Mai and south toward Surat Thani, the mainland gateway for the Gulf islands.

Bangkok to Chiang Mai takes about 12.5 to 13 hours, with services departing in the evening and arriving early the following morning.

Bangkok toward Surat Thani takes about 11 to 13 hours.

Accommodation is in first or second class air-conditioned sleepers with upper and lower berths; fan-cooled options exist on some services. Popular berths need booking weeks ahead.

The station changed

Long-distance services in all directions now run from Krung Thep Aphiwat Central Terminal. Hua Lamphong, the station named in most older guides and still fixed in a lot of published itineraries, is no longer the primary long-distance terminus.

Anyone planning from a guide written before the change would arrive at the wrong station.

What each does to the day around it

This is where the two diverge most, and it has nothing to do with the journey time.

A flight consumes part of a day at both ends — travel to the airport, the flight, travel from it. The day it lands in is a partial day.

An overnight train consumes a night and arrives early in the morning. It also removes a night of accommodation from the trip, and delivers a traveller into a full day at the destination rather than a partial one — though a full day begun on whatever sleep the berth allowed.

So the comparison is not one hour against thirteen. It is a partial day plus a hotel night, against a night in a berth and a full day on the ground.

Booking mechanics

Sleeper berths sell out weeks in advance on popular routes, so the train is the leg that has to be committed to early. Domestic flights are generally available closer in, at fares that move with demand.

Fares for both move enough that they are worth checking live rather than planning against a remembered figure:

100 USD ≈ … THB (enable JavaScript for today's rate)

Where this sits in a trip

The choice looks like a transport question and behaves like an itinerary question. It determines which day the destination begins, whether a hotel night is spent in Bangkok or in a berth, how early one leg has to be committed, and — if the flight leaves from the other airport — whether a 50 km road transfer sits in the middle of it.

Those consequences land in different parts of the plan and are decided at different times. How they fit together is worked through in the complete Thailand trip guide.

FAQ

How long is the overnight train from Bangkok to Chiang Mai?

About 12.5 to 13 hours, departing in the evening and arriving early the next morning.

Which Bangkok station do long-distance trains leave from?

Krung Thep Aphiwat Central Terminal serves all long-distance directions. Hua Lamphong, named in most older guides, is no longer the primary long-distance terminus.

How far ahead do I need to book a sleeper berth?

Weeks ahead on popular routes. Domestic flights are generally available closer to the date, at fares that move with demand.

How long is the flight from Bangkok to Chiang Mai?

About an hour in the air, with airport time at both ends — and a 50 km road transfer if the departure airport is not the one you arrived into.

What classes are on Thai sleeper trains?

First and second class air-conditioned sleepers with upper and lower berths, plus fan-cooled options on some services.

title: Getting Around Thailand: Flights, Trains, and Buses
excerpt: A complete overview of how to travel around Thailand — domestic flights, trains, buses, ferries, and local transport — with how to choose the right option for each journey.
content:
Thailand is a large country with excellent, affordable transport, and getting between regions is easier than first-timers expect. The main question on any journey is whether to prioritize speed (fly), scenery and romance (train), or budget (bus). Here's a complete overview of your options and when to use each.

Domestic flights — fastest for long distances

For covering Thailand's big distances — Bangkok to Chiang Mai, or Bangkok to the southern islands — flying is usually the smart choice. A competitive market (Thai AirAsia, Nok Air, Thai Lion Air, Bangkok Airways, Thai Airways, Thai Vietjet) keeps fares low, and flights take 1–1.5 hours versus 10+ hours overland. On a trip of two weeks or less, the time saved is almost always worth it. Just watch which Bangkok airport (Suvarnabhumi or Don Mueang) your flight uses.

Trains — scenic and characterful

Thailand's State Railway network is slower than flying but full of character. The standout is the overnight sleeper train from Bangkok to Chiang Mai — an atmospheric, comfortable way to travel north that saves a hotel night. Trains also run south toward Surat Thani (for the Gulf islands) and to the northeast. They're affordable and a genuine experience, ideal when the journey is part of the trip rather than just a transfer. Book sleeper berths ahead, especially in peak season.

Buses and minivans — cheapest and most extensive

Thailand's intercity bus network is vast, cheap, and reaches places trains and planes don't. VIP and first-class coaches are surprisingly comfortable for long hauls, including overnight routes, while minivans connect smaller towns and fill the gaps. Buses are the budget backbone of Thai travel; the trade-off is time and, on some routes, comfort. Use reputable operators and the government BKS terminals where possible.

Ferries — for the islands

Reaching the islands means a boat — ferries, speedboats, or longtails from mainland piers, often via combined bus-and-ferry or flight-and-ferry tickets. The Andaman coast (Phuket, Krabi) and the Gulf (Samui, Phangan, Tao) have separate ferry hubs, and crossings depend on the season's weather. Combined tickets make island connections simple. The key planning point is that the two coasts are reached differently and have opposite weather, so build your island legs around the season — the Andaman side in roughly November to April, the Gulf side around mid-year — to get the calmest, most reliable crossings.

Getting around locally

Within cities and towns, your options are Grab (the dominant ride-hailing app, great in cities, patchier on some islands), songthaews (shared pickup trucks on fixed or negotiated routes), tuk-tuks (fun but negotiate hard), metered taxis (insist on the meter), and Bangkok's excellent BTS Skytrain and MRT metro. On islands, many travelers rent scooters, though that carries real safety and insurance risks without a proper license.

What about renting a car or scooter?

Self-driving is less common among visitors to Thailand than in many countries, and for good reason. Thais drive on the left, city traffic is heavy and assertive, and you'll need an International Driving Permit alongside your home license. Many travelers find Grab, taxis, and intercity transport simpler and cheaper than renting a car, and skip the stress. Scooters are hugely popular on the islands for their freedom and low cost, but they're also the leading cause of tourist injury — roads can be rough, and your travel insurance may not cover a crash without a proper motorcycle license. Weigh that carefully before renting one.

How to choose for each journey

The simple framework: fly for long distances when time matters; take the overnight train when you want the experience and want to save a hotel night; take a bus or minivan when you're on a tight budget or going somewhere flights and trains don't reach; and use ferries for the islands. For a typical first trip with limited time, flying between regions and using Grab and trains locally covers almost everything. Fares are low across the board; check a live converter rather than a fixed figure:
